title: Wangchuk Hunger Strike Draws Global Solidarity as NEET Protests Become Modi's Biggest Challenge
excerpt: From Jantar Mantar to Union Square in New York, the youth-led movement over exam paper leaks has escalated into the largest demonstrations against the Indian government in years, with protests spreading to London, Dublin, and San Jose.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike has entered its 21st day, leading to hospitalization.
  • The Cockroach Janta Party's July 20 march was the largest protest against PM Modi's government in years.
  • International solidarity protests occurred in cities like London, Dublin, New York, and San Jose.
  • Protesters demand the resignation of the Education Minister and compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide.

What began as a sit-in by a satirically named student group has escalated into the most significant challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government in years, with climate activist Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike drawing international solidarity protests and the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party staging the largest demonstrations New Delhi has seen in over a decade.

Wangchuk, 59, was shifted from the protest site at Jantar Mantar to Safdarjung Hospital on July 18 after his health deteriorated on the 21st day of his indefinite fast. The Delhi High Court ordered the move, but protesters attempted to block police from removing him, leading to scuffles that further galvanised the movement. He has since been transferred to a private hospital.

A Movement Born From an Insult

The Cockroach Janta Party was founded by Boston University graduate Abhijeet Dipke after India's chief justice made comments in May that many interpreted as referring to the nation's unemployed youth as "cockroaches." The remark struck a nerve in a country where youth unemployment remains stubbornly high, and the CJP quickly channelled that anger toward a specific grievance: the alleged leak of NEET-UG 2026 exam papers.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2079533094412136956

The leak, which forced approximately two million students to re-sit the medical entrance examination, has had devastating consequences. Around 12 students who had been preparing for the exam have died by suicide, according to media reports. The CJP says the leak was emblematic of deep-seated corruption in India's education system, citing 152 paper leaks over the past decade with what Congress leader Rahul Gandhi called "zero convictions."

"All these leaders in power are illiterate and I am here to protest because we do not want question papers to leak. This should come to an end."

— Adi Nathan, 21, student from Meerut

Parliament March Turns Violent

The July 20 "Chalo Sansad" march on Parliament — timed to coincide with the opening day of the monsoon session — marked a dramatic escalation. Thousands of young supporters gathered through the night at Jantar Mantar before attempting to march toward the Parliament complex.

Delhi Police had imposed prohibitory orders and declared the march unlawful. Reuters journalists reported that security officers fired rounds of tear gas near Parliament to disperse protesters, while television images showed police baton charges. About 150 protesters were taken to hospital with injuries, according to CJP leaders. Delhi Police said 118 of its officers were also injured.

The protests disrupted proceedings on the opening day of the monsoon session, forcing the closure of Parliament gates and triggering repeated adjournments in both houses. By evening, police cleared the Jantar Mantar protest site, demolishing the makeshift camp that had served as the movement's headquarters. Protesters returned the next day and rebuilt it.

Global Diaspora Rallies in Support

The movement has resonated with the Indian diaspora, prompting solidarity demonstrations in multiple countries. Activists from Hindus for Human Rights gathered at the Mahatma Gandhi statue in New York's Union Square and in San Jose on Monday evening. Similar protests were held outside the Indian High Commission in London and the Indian Embassy in Dublin.

"Our protests sent a clear message, whether in New York or London, San Jose or Dublin: India's students deserve to be treated with fairness and dignity," the advocacy group said in a statement.

Anti-corruption activist Anna Hazare, who staged his own landmark hunger strike at Jantar Mantar in 2011, wrote to PM Modi saying the news of violence against protesters was "extremely painful" and urging the government to view the resentment "not as a law and order problem, but as the agony and expectations of society."

Wangchuk has laid out three conditions for ending his fast: the government must take responsibility for failures in the education system, guarantee that no legal action will be taken against peaceful protesters, and meet with him in hospital to assure him these conditions will be honoured.

Health Minister J.P. Nadda met a two-member CJP delegation and has asked for time to discuss their demands within the government. Modi, who rarely responds to public criticism, sent a message via the minister of parliamentary affairs saying he was committed to ensuring no more paper leaks. But with protesters vowing to continue their sit-in until demands are met, and opposition parties seizing the moment, the pressure on the government shows no sign of easing.
image_caption: Climate activist and education reformer Sonam Wangchuk, who has been on an indefinite hunger strike since June 28. Wangchuk was forcibly moved to hospital on July 18 after his health deteriorated, sparking wider protests.
nri_angle: Solidarity protests in New York, San Jose, London, and Dublin show the Indian diaspora's deepening engagement with domestic political movements, particularly around education and youth issues.
